recent.question: George Pickens: 1+ touchdowns
recent.what_happened: George Pickens, Dallas's WR1 in a home game against a weak 0-4 Tampa Bay team, scored at least one touchdown, so the market resolved YES. The market had priced this at about 41.5%; we had it at 23%.
recent.what_we_missed: The research was about the wrong thing. It collected base rates for defensive and special-teams touchdowns and nothing on Pickens himself: his target share, his red-zone usage, his touchdown rate (8+ receiving TDs in 2025) or Tampa Bay's injury-hit secondary (Winfield and Morrison out). For a top receiver in a favorable matchup, the right base rate for an anytime TD is about 35–45%.
recent.lesson: For a player-prop TD market, start from the player's own touchdown rate and the market's implied price, and use team or D/ST base rates only when the market is about a team or a defense.

suggested_change.change: Before research starts, check that the subject of the research matches the market's subject, here the named player rather than a defense or special-teams unit. When the forecast differs from a liquid market by more than 15 points with no player-specific evidence behind it, flag the forecast.

recent.question: Full Game: over 47.5 points scored? (Over 47.5 points)
recent.what_happened: Tampa Bay won 24-16, its first win of the season, for 40 total points, which is under 47.5. Dak Prescott threw two interceptions and Dallas struggled against the Bucs' blitz. Dallas led only 10-7 at halftime, and Tampa Bay's two touchdowns from Bucky Irving plus a long Tez Johnson catch didn't add up to a shootout.
recent.what_we_missed: The forecast gave too much weight to Dallas's four straight overs from a four-game sample. It gave too little weight to the Tampa Bay side: an undrafted rookie quarterback making his first road start on a short week, a Bucs defense ranked 4th in total yards, and three straight Bucs games totaling 42 or fewer points. That evidence supported the market's roughly 52% or lower, not 64%.
recent.lesson: When a total is set near the market's fair line and the two teams' recent scoring trends point in opposite directions, do not move far from the market because one team's games went over in a 3-4 game streak, especially when the other team has a backup quarterback and a strong defense.

suggested_change.change: Cap how far a game-total forecast can move from the market (for example, 5 points) unless there is concrete new information the market hasn't priced, such as a late injury or weather; a scoring streak over a few games doesn't count.

recent.question: Dallas wins
recent.what_happened: Tampa Bay, previously winless, won 24-16 at Dallas. Undrafted rookie QB Jalon Daniels completed 19 of 25 passes for 189 yards with no turnovers. Bucky Irving ran for 165 yards and 2 TDs, including a 72-yard run that set up the go-ahead score, and Dak Prescott threw 2 interceptions.
recent.what_we_missed: Nothing decisive was knowable before kickoff. The research forecast of 0.63 was already well below the market's 0.795 because Dallas's defense ranked near the bottom of the league (30th in yards allowed, 29th in points allowed) and the Bucs' defense was strong. Turnovers and one long run decided the game, and those are mostly random.
recent.lesson: When a heavy favorite has a bottom-tier run defense and its opponent has a strong defense plus a backup QB who protects the ball, discount the favorite's chances as the research forecast did, and don't treat an upset like this as a modeling failure.

suggested_change.change: Keep weighting defensive mismatches against market favorites as the research forecast did here; the outcome was variance.

recent.question: Tampa Bay wins
recent.what_happened: Tampa Bay won 24-16 at Dallas for its first win of the season. Bucky Irving ran for 165 yards and two TDs, rookie Jalon Daniels managed the game well (19 of 25, 189 yards, 1 TD), and Dak Prescott threw two interceptions.
recent.what_we_missed: Nothing that could have been known. The underdog won, and the 0.27 forecast was already above the market's 0.205. Every Bucs loss had been by 7 points or fewer, the Bucs had a top-five run defense, and Dallas was 2-2 with a leaky defense, so an upset was always plausible.
recent.lesson: When a pregame market is priced more lopsided than the spread suggests (one preview had Dallas at -3.5, which usually means about a 35-38% win chance for the underdog, versus 20.5% here), give the spread weight and lean toward the underdog. Don't let the backup-QB story drag the probability down too far.

suggested_change.change: Pull the point spread and moneyline from several sportsbooks and convert them to implied probabilities, then use that as a check on the Kalshi price before shading below it.

recent.question: Javonte Williams: 1+ touchdowns
recent.what_happened: Javonte Williams, Dallas's lead back with 6 TDs in 4 games, scored at least one touchdown at home against the 0-4 Buccaneers, so the market resolved YES. My searches found no game recap to confirm the details, so this rests on the stated outcome. The market had priced YES at 64.5%.
recent.what_we_missed: Most of the research was about defensive and special-teams touchdowns: league D/ST base rates, punt-return touchdowns, and Dallas's lack of interceptions. That doesn't matter for whether a running back scores. It looks like the question was read as being about a D/ST touchdown. The one relevant fact was that Williams had 6 TDs in 4 games, about 1.5 per game, as the featured back facing a weak, turnover-prone opponent. That supports a probability of 60–70%, not 23–43%.
recent.lesson: For an 'anytime TD' prop on a player, start from that player's own TD rate, red-zone role and team's implied point total, and treat a large gap from the market as a sign you've misread the question.

suggested_change.change: Classify the question by subject (an offensive skill player vs. a team D/ST), then require player-specific stats such as TDs per game, red-zone carries and snap share, plus the betting line, before any base rates are pulled.

recent.question: Milwaukee wins
recent.what_happened: Milwaukee won Game 4 3-1 at Petco Park and eliminated San Diego. Garrett Mitchell tripled and scored the go-ahead run on Jackson Chourio's single in the fifth. Aaron Ashby threw three scoreless innings in relief of Robert Gasser, and the win ended the Brewers' 12-game postseason road losing streak.
recent.what_we_missed: The research-based forecast dropped to 0.30, about 20 points below a roughly 50/50 market. It leaned on weak signals: a franchise-history road skid with no bearing on this roster, and an unannounced Brewers starter. It gave too little weight to the facts that cut the other way: the Padres' bullpen was depleted, with Mason Miller on the paternity list, Adrian Morejon unavailable and Michael King used on short rest; Milwaukee had several rested relievers; and the Brewers won 103 games and went 48-33 on the road.
recent.lesson: If a ballgame's market is near a coin flip and the evidence points both ways, stay close to the market price, and don't let franchise-history streaks or narrative base rates move the forecast far from it.

suggested_change.change: Cap how far a forecast can move from the market (for example, 10 points) on single-game sports markets, unless there is concrete new information such as an injury or lineup change the market hasn't priced in. Give near-zero weight to franchise-history streaks that don't reflect the current roster.

recent_wins.question: DAL Cowboys wins by over 9.5 points?
recent_wins.what_happened: Tampa Bay beat Dallas 24-16 in Arlington on October 8, 2026, its first win of the season. Rookie QB Jalon Daniels went 19 of 25 for 189 yards with no turnovers, Bucky Irving ran for a career-high 165 yards, and Dak Prescott threw two interceptions. Dallas didn't win at all, so the 9.5-point cover resolved No.
recent_wins.what_worked: The forecast was only slightly below the market (0.42 vs 0.475) and still leaned Yes-ish. The evidence pointing down was real: all four Bucs losses were by 7 points or fewer, Tampa Bay's run defense ranked 4th in total defense and 3rd against the run, Dallas's defense was 29th–31st, and only one of Dallas's four games was a 10+ point win. Even so, an 8-point outright upset is not something a 42% forecast predicted. This was close to a coin flip that went our way.
recent_wins.lesson: When a team keeps losing close games and has a top run defense, discount big spreads against it even with a backup QB, but treat an edge of about 5 points over the market as small and don't count the result as proof the reasoning was right.

suggested_change.change: For spread questions, have research pull each team's distribution of final margins and its record against the spread, so the forecast rests on more than injury news and the market price.

recent_wins.question: New York Y vs Tampa Bay Division Series winner: New York Y wins
recent_wins.what_happened: Tampa Bay swept the Yankees 3-0. In Game 3 at Yankee Stadium on Oct 7 the Rays won 4-3: Victor Mesa Jr. hit a two-run homer off Max Fried in the 6th, and a fan interference call took away a possible game-tying Anthony Volpe home run.
recent_wins.what_worked: The research found that the series stood at 2-0 for Tampa Bay, so the Yankees had to win three straight against a 98-win top seed. That took the forecast from the uninformed 0.51 down to 0.19. Teams down 0-2 in a best-of-five come back only about 10-15% of the time, so this was mostly a solid read of the current state, not a close call.
recent_wins.lesson: For series markets, check the current series score and whether a game is in progress before anything else, then start from the historical comeback rate for that deficit.

suggested_change.change: Our 0.19 was still above the market's 0.08 at a judgment time (10:05 PM EDT) when Game 3 was probably already underway. Block or shrink bets toward YES while a deciding game is live, because the market price likely reflects in-game information our research doesn't have.

recent_wins.question: Will Clube do Remo win on 2026-10-07?
recent_wins.what_happened: Remo and Grêmio drew 1-1 at the Mangueirão on 2026-10-07. Kannemann scored for Grêmio around the end of the first half and David Braga equalised late, around the 88th minute, so the market resolved No. Remo now have 11 straight games without a win.
recent_wins.what_worked: The research found Remo's collapse in form: ten games without a win, five straight one-goal league losses, five home games without a win, and a record of never beating Grêmio. That correctly argued against the market's 46.5%, which seemed to be pricing mostly home advantage and Grêmio's poor away record. Still, 19% was probably too confident. Remo were pressing for a winner late, and the 36-37% estimates made without the research would also have beaten the market, so part of the edge came from the market being overpriced rather than from precision.
recent_wins.lesson: When a relegation-zone home side is on a long winless run and has a new coach in his first home game, a near coin-flip market price for a home win is often too high. Bet against it, but size the edge closer to a 30-35% chance than to 19%.

suggested_change.change: Before final weighting, sort out source conflicts on suspensions and returns (here Jajá's return and whether Marllon was suspended), so form-based downgrades aren't stacked on top of lineup penalties that may be stale.

recent_wins.question: Atlanta wins
recent_wins.what_happened: The Dodgers won Game 4 4-1 at Truist Park and took the NLDS 3-1. The game was tied 1-1 until the 7th, when Andy Pages hit a two-run, bases-loaded single off Robert Suarez. Max Muncy added a solo homer in the 9th.
recent_wins.what_worked: Taking research into account, the forecast was 0.27, below both the market (0.425) and the no-research estimate (0.46). The direction was correct, and the facts that supported it were real: Glasnow's strikeout rate, Acuña's knee injury, the slumps of Acuña and Baldwin, and a strong Dodgers team. The game itself was a coin flip through six innings, though. The 70% series figure in the research describes the whole series, not Game 4, and Mahle had a 1.99 ERA for Atlanta after the trade. A home team's chance in one game should not fall to 27% on this evidence.
recent_wins.lesson: If a single-game forecast moves more than about 10 points away from a liquid moneyline, write down a specific fact the market is mispricing. Without one, treat a winning result as noise, not as proof the method works.

suggested_change.change: Shrink single-game MLB forecasts toward the market price unless research finds a concrete fact the market hasn't priced, such as a late lineup scratch or a change of starter, and flag any use of series-level base rates as a single-game probability.

recent_wins.question: Will Mexico win on 2026-10-05?
recent_wins.what_happened: The friendly was played on October 6, 2026 at the LA Memorial Coliseum, one day after the date in the question. Chile beat Mexico 2-0 with goals from Maximiliano Gutiérrez (56') and Vicente Pizarro (66'). That left Mexico without a win in four games under Rafa Márquez, and the market resolved No.
recent_wins.what_worked: The research forecast moved from 0.40 to 0.16 on real warning signs: Mexico had won none of three games under Márquez, had leaked goals against the US, was missing four players (Mora, Chávez, Lozano, Romo), and might change goalkeepers. It also correctly noted that a draw counts as No. Still, nothing found before kickoff decided the game. A pro-Mexico crowd in LA against a Chile team that had lost both of its window games made Mexico's win chance roughly 45-60%, so 0.16 was far too confident and mostly got lucky against the market's 0.625.
recent_wins.lesson: If the forecast differs from the market by more than 30 points and no decisive fact (lineup collapse, rule quirk, known result) is behind it, pull it back toward the market. Poor form and injuries in a friendly don't justify a 4-to-1 call against the favourite.

suggested_change.change: Add a check that flags any forecast more than 30 points from the market unless the research cites a specific fact that decides the outcome, and caps how big a bet it can drive.

recent_wins.question: Will Jackson Olson and their partner be eliminated from Dancing with the Stars Season 35 before Oct 7, 2026?
recent_wins.what_happened: On Mariah Carey Night (Oct 6), Jackson Olson and Emma Slater danced a Waltz to 'Without You' and scored 21/30, their best score so far. Only Ciara Miller and Brandon Armstrong were eliminated, so Olson stayed in and the question resolved No.
recent_wins.what_worked: The forecast saw that only one live show fell inside the window and that every episode so far had sent home just one couple. That left one elimination among 12 couples. Olson was weak but not clearly the weakest: Guillermo Rodriguez kept scoring lower, and Ciara Miller had tied Olson at 18. So a probability around 22% made sense. The market's 61.5% was an overreaction to Olson being in the bottom three in Week 3.
recent_wins.lesson: For single-episode elimination markets, start from 1 divided by the number of couples left (times the eliminations expected that night), then adjust for judges' scores and bottom-three history. Being in the bottom three once rarely justifies a price above 50% when several other couples score as low or lower.

suggested_change.change: Always pull a full scoreboard of who has been in the bottom two or three and who has the lowest scores, plus how many eliminations are expected per episode, so the forecast can measure how weak the contestant really is against the rest of the field.

rules.rule: Read crypto rules for the exact strike, venue/pair (e.g. Binance BTC/USDT) and test (any touch or a close at a set candle), restate the strike up top, measure each price fact against it, and record a timestamped spot from that venue under an hour old for same-day windows.

For crypto threshold questions, report percent distance to strike, hours left, how many of the last 14 days the venue traded through that level, realized volatility, any weekend, and timestamped same-day catalysts (yields, dollar, ETF flows, jobs data) or state none found.

When judged mid-window, first check whether the strike was already reached inside the window: cite dated reports of the high and its margin past the strike, confirm on the resolution venue's candles where possible, and treat earlier-week moves as background.

For single-match win questions, confirm whether only a regulation-time win counts and that a draw resolves No; check the actual venue, and report each side's dated results in this competition, current winless or losing runs, and any recent coach change.

For match questions, report the current-season head-to-head with game count (under about 10 is small) and each side's dated absences, suspensions and returns; when sources disagree, settle it from the confirmed squad or lineup before citing it.
Discard any search snippet claiming a match result that is undated or dated before kickoff; report a result only from sources published after the match was played.

For match goal-total questions, report each team's recent comparable match totals with dates, note whether opponents in any blowout were weakened or missing starters, and compare that with the upcoming opponent's squad strength.

For tennis completion questions, read which endings count, report the tour level's normal-finish share and each player's recent full matches, weigh only past-week injury or withdrawal news, and after start time check Tennis Explorer or ITF for w/o or ret. first.

For NFL player props, use only the named player's facts: for TDs, rushing vs receiving, share of carries or targets inside the 5, multi-season TD-game rate; for yardage, current-season attempts per game, games past the line, opponent's rank against it, backfield injuries.

For single MMA fights, report each fighter's age, recent opponents and how those fights ended, and dated weigh-in or weight-cut news; label win streaks and common-opponent comparisons as weak evidence.

For single MLB games, report confirmed starters' ERA, ERA+ and recent starts, each bullpen's unavailable arms (injury, leave, short rest), season and road records, and form since Sept 1; label old-roster franchise streaks and series-level rates as not single-game evidence.

For playoff series, first get the live or final score of any game started before the judgment time, then report the series score, wins the trailer needs and where, the cited comeback rate for that deficit, game margins and season records; past seasons' playoffs are background.

For in-round golf leader questions, pull the live hole-by-hole leaderboard and, for the named player and everyone within about 3 shots, report score, holes left and tee wave, plus the field's scoring average and how the rules settle a tie for the lead.

For golf tournament winner questions, report the player's world ranking, pro starts and wins, the field's strength and size, and his prior-week schedule (e.g. a team event); label team-event results and a single pro win as weak evidence of dominance.

For video view questions, record when the question opened and check the channel's upload list for any video posted since; if one is live, report its upload time, hours elapsed, current views and climb rate before any historical base rates, plus sequel or promotion context.

For view-count bracket questions, build reference figures only from first-168-hour counts of the channel's recent comparable uploads; label cumulative or lifetime totals, figures with unclear snapshot dates, and months-old uploads as not the resolution metric.

For Rotten Tomatoes score questions, read the year-specific film page named in the rules, record the score, review count and dated earlier readings showing drift, and count how many negative reviews would move it past the strike before the check time.

For reality-show elimination questions, confirm every fact names the asked contestant and their own pro partner, and report couples left, eliminations per episode, live shows in the window, and every couple's judges' scores and bottom-three history.

For multi-seat or multi-candidate elections, report alongside polls the undecided share, joint tickets and endorsements, late dropouts and whom they backed, whether one side's vote splits across candidates, and dated past gaps between final polls and results there.

Take counts and base rates from a cited source covering the current format to the latest event, using the resolution's named provider and its counting method first (e.g. its trailing 2–4 weeks); label recalled, disputed or roughly dozen-case counts as unverified.

proposals.title: Claude direct sticks to sports and culture
proposals.why: Claude trails the market badly outside sports: politics 0.255 vs 0.117 (13 markets), weather 0.208 vs 0.072 (19), other 0.138 vs 0.099 (19), crypto 0.134 vs 0.110 (37). It beats the market in sports (0.161 vs 0.177, 146 markets) and probably in culture (0.040 vs 0.089, but only 5 markets). Since its edge rose to 12c it has settled only 2 bets, so this is an experiment. It also sets up a comparison with ch16: a strict sports Claude (12c edge, info gate 0.5) against a loose one (8c edge, info gate 0.2).
proposals.judge_by: On bets opened after this change, Claude direct's P&L per $100 staked is positive and beats its all-time -$55 per $100. We also compare it with ch16's over the same period to see whether the strict or the loose sports setup earns more per $100.
proposals.status_reason: claude_direct rules v4: skips none → crypto, economy, other, politics, tech, weather, world

proposals.title: Report settled stake separately from open stake
proposals.why: Most of our judge_by tests use 'P&L per $100 staked since the change', but the reported stake includes open bets. Bold has 14 of 41 bets open and ch16 has 8 of 10, so the per-$100 figures look better than they are. Splitting settled stake from open stake would let us judge p14, p18, p19, p21, p23 and p24 honestly.
proposals.judge_by: all_time, since_change and yardstick each report a settled_staked field, and the next review can compute P&L per $100 on settled bets only for every strategy.

proposals.title: Favourites-only challenger loosens its info gate
proposals.why: ch13 has placed only 5 bets in about 4.5 days. The 30 markets it skipped only because of Jev's info gate would have returned +$4.15 per $100 (19 wins), the only gate-blocked group in the ledger with a meaningful count that shows a profit. Lowering the gate from 0.5 to 0.35, bold's setting, should give it more bets at 55c and up. This is an experiment on noisy numbers.
proposals.judge_by: On bets opened after this change, ch13 places at least 2 bets a day, and its P&L per $100 staked is positive and no worse than calibrated's over the same period.

proposals.title: Main demands a bigger edge
proposals.why: Jev + research trails the market by about 0.06 Brier on 559 paired markets, so many of its 8c 'edges' are probably forecast error. Main loses about $26 per $100 since the floor (11 settled) and trails original per dollar on the yardstick (-$32 vs -$22 per $100). Requiring 12c, as claude_direct now does, tests whether fewer, stronger-conviction bets lose less. This is an experiment on small numbers.
proposals.judge_by: On bets opened after this change, main's P&L per $100 staked on the yardstick (shared markets) is better than original's over the same period, and better than main's since-floor -$26 per $100. If main places fewer than 10 bets in a week, revert to 0.08.

proposals.title: Price breakdown since each strategy's last rule change
proposals.why: by_price_paid is all-time, so pre-floor long shots dominate it: about $100k of losses on 73 bets. That hides whether 30-60c and 60c+ bets pay under the current rules. Bold's -$5.5k and calibrated's +$5.0k in favourites can't be dated to a rule version.
proposals.judge_by: The review shows since-change wins and P&L per price bucket for every strategy, and the next favourites or max_ask decision cites it.

proposals.title: Sports-only Claude gets more bets
proposals.why: Sports is the only category where any forecaster beats the market (Claude 0.158 vs market 0.176, on 131 markets), yet ch16 has placed 1 bet in about 2.5 days. The 4 markets stopped only by Jev's info gate would have paid +$77 per $100. Jev's own information rating may say little about Claude's forecast. This is an experiment on tiny numbers.
proposals.judge_by: On bets opened after this change, ch16's P&L per $100 staked is positive and ahead of claude_direct's over the same period.

proposals.title: Calibrated vs main on the same markets
proposals.why: Calibrated's profit (+$3.4k on 9 settled since the floor) contrasts with its Brier of 0.210, slightly worse than raw Jev + research at 0.2065. So its edge may come from which bets it picks and how it sizes them, or it may be luck. A paired comparison would show whether the calibration itself earns money before anyone considers moving main onto it.
proposals.judge_by: Report calibrated's and main's P&L per $100 on markets both bet, and on markets only one bet, since 2026-10-01. If calibrated is ahead by more than $10 per $100 on the shared markets after 30 resolved, consider giving main the calibrated forecasts.

proposals.title: Jev alone, bold stops buying favourites
proposals.why: Jev alone, bold has lost all 3 of its bets at 60c and up (-$6.0k), while its 30-60c bets are +$914 on 6. Jev alone is the weakest forecaster (Brier 0.235), and paying 60c+ leaves little room for its error. This rests on only 3 bets, so it is an experiment.
proposals.judge_by: On bets opened after this change, P&L per $100 staked beats its since-floor -$4.9 per $100 and its all-time -$43 per $100.
proposals.status_reason: jev_alone_bold rules v4: highest price none → 60¢

A strategy option that blends the forecast with the market price (for example 50/50) before the edge check would bet only where a disagreement survives that discount. The forecasters themselves would still never see the price.

rule_changes.why: Jev alone scores worse than the market in every category, with a Brier of 0.221 against 0.052 in crypto (21 resolved) and 0.294 against 0.168 in economy (12 resolved). This strategy has lost $17 per $100 staked (22 bets, 6 settled). The experiment is to demand a bigger edge and skip Jev's worst categories, while leaving the info gate at 0.2 so it stays distinct from Jev alone.
rule_changes.judge_by: On bets opened after this change, P&L per $100 staked beats its all-time -$17.4 per $100 and is at least as good as jev_alone over the same period.

rule_changes.why: Bold's extra bets, where Jev's info rating is 0.2–0.5, are losing $31.79 per $100 (7 bets), and main's info-stopped markets lose $70 per $100 (16). A 0.35 threshold tests where the cutoff really belongs, without collapsing bold into a copy of main.
rule_changes.judge_by: Bold's P&L per $100 staked since the change beats its old -$31.79 per $100, and is closer to or above main's over the same period.

rule_changes.why: In crypto the market scores a Brier of 0.034 against Jev+research's 0.117 (9 resolved), so any edge we think we see there is most likely our own error. This is an experiment on a small sample.
rule_changes.judge_by: On the yardstick, main's P&L on bets opened after this change is at least original's. Meanwhile, original's crypto bets over the same period lose money in total.

ideas_for_joey.title: Break results down by price paid
ideas_for_joey.why: Many losses, including all 3 of claude_direct's and every info-gate-stopped group, show -$100 per $100, meaning the whole stake was lost. That pattern suggests we may be buying cheap longshots. A breakdown of wins and P&L by ask price (for example <0.2, 0.2–0.5, 0.5–0.8, >0.8), for placed and stopped bets, would let us set min_ask and max_ask from evidence instead of guessing.

ideas_for_joey.title: Score forecasters on 30c+ markets only
ideas_for_joey.why: Since 2026-10-01 every strategy bets only at 30c or more, but the Brier table (market 0.114 vs our best 0.121) mixes in the long shots we no longer touch. We need to know whether any forecaster beats the price where we actually bet, matched market by market.

ideas_for_joey.title: Shrink forecasts toward the market before computing edge
ideas_for_joey.why: The market's Brier (0.123, 201 markets) beats every forecaster, and most of our losses came from bets where we disagreed with it most, such as long shots that went 1 for 21. A strategy option that blends the forecast with the market price (for example 50/50) before the edge check would bet only where a disagreement survives that discount. The forecasters themselves would still never see the price.

ideas_for_joey.title: Gate ledger and price breakdown for 30c+ markets only
ideas_for_joey.why: The gate ledger mixes in long shots, which lost 1 in 42 before the floor. That makes every 'stopped by the info gate' number look worse than it would under today's rules: calibrated's info-stopped markets show −$7.1 per $100 (66) and main's −$24.6 (78). We can't sensibly tune the info gates until the ledger shows only markets the 30c floor would let through.

ideas_for_joey.title: Pooled tally of bets placed under the floor
ideas_for_joey.why: Each strategy has 0–1 settled bets since 2026-10-01, so the floor's '30 settled bets' test will take weeks per strategy. Pooling every strategy's 30c+ bets placed since the floor, measured against original's long shots over the same period, would answer whether the floor pays much sooner.

ideas_for_joey.title: Claimed edge vs realised return
ideas_for_joey.why: Every source is worse than the market, yet each bet claims at least 8c of edge. Bucketing settled 30c+ bets by claimed edge (8-12c, 12-20c, 20c+) and showing win rate and P&L per $100 would show whether big claimed edges are real edges or big errors. That would tell us whether to raise or lower min_edge.

ideas_for_joey.title: Calibrated vs main on the same markets
ideas_for_joey.why: Calibrated's profit (+$3.4k on 9 settled since the floor) contrasts with its Brier of 0.210, slightly worse than raw Jev + research at 0.2065. So its edge may come from which bets it picks and how it sizes them, or it may be luck. A paired comparison would show whether the calibration itself earns money before anyone considers moving main onto it.

ideas_for_joey.title: Price breakdown since each strategy's last rule change
ideas_for_joey.why: by_price_paid is all-time, so pre-floor long shots dominate it: about $100k of losses on 73 bets. That hides whether 30-60c and 60c+ bets pay under the current rules. Bold's -$5.5k and calibrated's +$5.0k in favourites can't be dated to a rule version.

ideas_for_joey.title: Report settled stake separately from open stake
ideas_for_joey.why: Most of our judge_by tests use 'P&L per $100 staked since the change', but the reported stake includes open bets. Bold has 14 of 41 bets open and ch16 has 8 of 10, so the per-$100 figures look better than they are. Splitting settled stake from open stake would let us judge p14, p18, p19, p21, p23 and p24 honestly.
